verification.note: Abstract read: an analysis of “the concept of working-class culture as applied by some practitioners of the new labour history in Canada”; questions “the validity of using such a general framework” — the evidence at times supports working-class culture as an important determinant and at other times does not; argues that to insist history be studied “from the bottom up” is “as predeterministic as the notion that it should be studied ‘from the top down.’” Published in the issue’s Critiques section; Kealey replies in the same issue (wcreq_kealey_1981). Checked against: Labour/Le Travail article page with abstract, https://lltjournal.ca/index.php/llt/article/view/2658 (read 2026-10-12); Crossref DOI record (JSTOR); answers/verification.json Q29. Addendum 2026-10-13: Full text read (Érudit PDF, id.erudit.org/iderudit/llt7cri02, pp. 95–112). p. 97: Canadian practitioners of the new labour history “follow the thinking of E.P. Thompson in Britain, Herbert Gutman in the United States, and others in applying the culturalist approach to Canadian experience”; “Palmer, echoing E.P. Thompson, regards culture and conflict as ‘complementary processes’” (citing A Culture in Conflict, p. xii, which was not itself checked). p. 98: in Canada new labour historians “stand in the middle but so far tend to lean to the British experience. They study working-class culture for the explanation and definition they believe it offers in the Thompson sense”. p. 108: “Even if Thompson is right about England, his concepts do not necessarily apply anywhere else.” A critic’s characterization, not a self-description.

karl.label: Historical materialism
karl.date_label: Marx’s preface 1859 · Capital I 1867 · later Marxists
karl.description: Modes of production, relations of exploitation, class struggle, and historically specific capitalism. Later Marxists disagree over determinism, agency, and culture. Marx’s 1859 developmental propositions coexist with his 1877 rejection of a universal path. Later debates concern political action, imperial accumulation, dialectical and analytical explanation, and reproduction of material life.
karl.representative_figures_and_works: Karl Marx (1818–1883), Capital I (1867); developed in critical engagement with political economy, philosophy, and socialist movements.

representative_people.context: Analyzes historically specific production and exploitation. The 1859 preface advances strong forces/relations propositions; the 1877 Russian letter rejects exporting the Western-European expropriation account as a universal path. These claims require comparison, not silent harmonization.
representative_people.works: Capital I (1867); preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy (1859); Russian editorial-board letter (1877)

representative_people.context: A specific historical use of capitalism, wage labor and family dependence to explain sexual identity; not an assertion of formal school membership or a universal cause.
representative_people.works: “Capitalism and Gay Identity” (1983)

representative_people.context: Translation, annotation and selection make Marxist texts available in particular political and pedagogical settings; editorial mediation is a substantive contribution.
representative_people.works: Marx–Engels Selected Correspondence (English translation, 1934); supplementary notes to Capital I (1938); Marx on China (introduction and notes, 1951)

representative_people.context: Uses Capital’s production and rent categories in a contested historical explanation; his reply recognizes varied forms and limits in his own evidence.
representative_people.works: Studies in the Development of Capitalism (1946); reply to Sweezy in “The Transition from Feudalism to Capitalism” (1950), pp. 157–167

representative_people.context: A contested philosophical rereading of Marx: problematics, overdetermination and the relation of knowledge to its object. His own later foreword qualifies theoreticism.
representative_people.works: For Marx and Reading Capital (1965); revised Reading Capital foreword (1968/1970)

representative_people.context: Contributor to the five-author Reading Capital; the consulted abridged edition retains Althusser and Balibar while omitting Rancière, Macherey and Establet. Coauthorship does not imply identical positions or later agreement.
representative_people.works: Reading Capital (1965), authorship and edition history in the revised foreword (1968/1970)

representative_people.context: Contributor to the five-author Reading Capital; the consulted abridged edition retains Althusser and Balibar while omitting Rancière, Macherey and Establet. Coauthorship does not imply identical positions or later agreement.
representative_people.works: Reading Capital (1965), authorship and edition history in the revised foreword (1968/1970)

representative_people.context: Contributor to the five-author Reading Capital; the consulted abridged edition retains Althusser and Balibar while omitting Rancière, Macherey and Establet. Coauthorship does not imply identical positions or later agreement.
representative_people.works: Reading Capital (1965), authorship and edition history in the revised foreword (1968/1970)

representative_people.context: Contributor to the five-author Reading Capital; the consulted abridged edition retains Althusser and Balibar while omitting Rancière, Macherey and Establet. Coauthorship does not imply identical positions or later agreement.
representative_people.works: Reading Capital (1965), authorship and edition history in the revised foreword (1968/1970)

representative_people.context: Althusser explicitly credits Martin for the concept of the problematic. This is a named conceptual resource in an authorial acknowledgment, not an independently read Martin text or claim of founding a school.
representative_people.works: Acknowledgment in Althusser, For Marx, introduction (1965), section II

representative_people.context: Collaborates with Marx. His Bloch letter rejects an economic-only explanation and gives political struggles and individual wills effects, while retaining economic determination in the last instance.
representative_people.works: Letter to Joseph Bloch (21–22 September 1890); collaboration described in Marx’s 1859 preface

representative_people.context: Presents dialectical method and historically conditioned facts as central, with theory/practice inseparable. His criticism of Engels and strong claims for dialectical truth distinguish this program from generic pluralism.
representative_people.works: What is Orthodox Marxism? (1919), in History and Class Consciousness (1923), opening and sections 1–2

representative_people.context: Treats political violence and exchanges with noncapitalist settings as ongoing aspects of accumulation. Her disagreement with Engels and her collapse thesis remain specific, contestable positions.
representative_people.works: The Accumulation of Capital (1913), chapter 31

representative_people.context: Develops an account of monopoly, finance and imperial conflict, with an explicit political purpose and a censorship history. The 1920 preface’s predictions are his arguments, not a consensus of all Marxists.
representative_people.works: Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism (1916/1917), 1920 French/German preface and book introduction

representative_people.context: Offers an analytical reconstruction, distinguishing what Marx held about productive-force primacy from reasons to defend it; functional explanation is part of the proposed account. The 2000 edition adds reservations.
representative_people.works: Karl Marx’s Theory of History: A Defence (1978; expanded 2000), description and displayed chapter openings

representative_people.context: Reworks Marxian categories for gender and production/reproduction of material life. This selection records the stated feminist project; its specific mechanism awaits a body-passage check.
representative_people.works: Marxism and the Oppression of Women: Toward a Unitary Theory (1983), publisher description

representative_people.context: Marx retrospectively identifies critical reexamination of Hegel’s philosophy of law as a step toward his investigation of material relations. This is a specified critical resource, not adherence to the whole Hegelian system.
representative_people.works: Philosophy of law, discussed in Marx’s 1859 preface

representative_people.context: Investigates class as a historical relationship made through activity and experience; the previously checked preface resists treating workers only as industrial inputs.
representative_people.works: The Making of the English Working Class (1963), preface

representative_people.context: Distinguishes materialist method from conclusions about nineteenth-century Europe and asks how to investigate African histories in their own time and place.
representative_people.works: Marxism and African Liberation (1975 speech)

representative_people.context: Reworks materialist resources in the history of slavery and revolution. His later lectures name Marx, Lenin and Trotsky as readings; retrospective chronology retains its limits.
representative_people.works: The Black Jacobins (1938); Lectures on The Black Jacobins (1971)

representative_people.context: Political-class account discussed critically in Gramsci’s inquiry into intellectual functions.
representative_people.works: Elementi di scienza politica (expanded edition1923), Gramsci author noteA

representative_people.context: An explicitly compared theorist; this selection does not imply Marxist affiliation.
representative_people.works: Theory of elites, compared in Gramsci’s Intellectuals author noteA

representative_people.context: Editorial and translation work enables a particular English selection; translated history, education and politics.
representative_people.works: Selections from the Prison Notebooks (1971), co-editor/translator, prefaceix–xv

representative_people.context: Translated intellectuals, Fordism and philosophy; editorial arrangement differs from notebook sequence.
representative_people.works: Selections from the Prison Notebooks (1971), co-editor/translator, prefaceix–xv

karl.scope_note: Marx’s historical materialism must be distinguished from the competing historical programmes of later Marxists. Neither Marx’s late qualification nor Engels’s acknowledgment of political effects cancels their stronger causal claims. Lukács, Luxemburg, Lenin, Althusser, Cohen and feminist reworkings offer distinct arguments; shared materialist resources do not establish one doctrine or a verified world chronology.

strands.title: Translation, annotation and historical use
strands.focus: Torr’s editions mediate Marxist writings; Dobb’s reply applies and debates particular rent/production categories. Making texts available and accepting every historical interpretation are different activities.
strands.works: Selected Correspondence (1934); Capital I notes (1938); Dobb reply (1950); Marx on China (1951)

strands.title: Problematics and a disputed epistemological break
strands.focus: Althusser distinguishes changing theoretical questions from merely changing words, credits Martin and Bachelard, and disputes rival periodizations of Marx.

strands.title: Collective reading and theoretical self-criticism
strands.focus: The 1965 seminar produces distinct incomplete readings. Later abridgment and a qualification of theoreticism should not be projected backward as a unified original position.
strands.works: Reading Capital (1965), revised foreword and selected Part I (1968/1970)

strands.title: Overdetermination and political circumstances
strands.focus: Althusser gives political and ideological circumstances explanatory force while retaining economic determination in the last instance. Gramsci is a named resource; reductionism and agency remain disputed.

strands.title: Production relations and the scope of historical claims
strands.focus: Marx’s 1859 preface advances developmental propositions; the 1877 letter restricts the expropriation account to Western Europe and requires comparison of different outcomes. The tension remains visible.

strands.title: Political struggle and economic determination
strands.focus: Engels gives politics, law, theory and individual wills causal effects while maintaining economic determination in the last instance. This qualification is neither economic-only causation nor abandonment of materialism.

strands.title: Dialectical method and historical practice
strands.focus: Lukács treats facts as historically conditioned and connects theory with practice; criticism of Engels coexists with strong claims for dialectical truth.
strands.works: What is Orthodox Marxism? (1919/1923), opening and sections 1–2

strands.title: Different accounts of accumulation and imperial power
strands.focus: Luxemburg’s noncapitalist relations/violence argument and Lenin’s monopoly/finance framing are distinct. Their revolutionary predictions remain attributed propositions rather than independently established historical laws.
strands.works: Accumulation of Capital, chapter 31 (1913); Imperialism, 1920 preface

strands.title: Analytical reconstruction and revision
strands.focus: Cohen separates textual interpretation from defending productive-force primacy and presents functional explanation as part of his reconstruction. The 2000 edition’s reservations qualify its relation to 1978.
strands.works: Karl Marx’s Theory of History (1978/2000), displayed chapter openings

strands.title: Gender and reproduction of material life
strands.focus: Vogel’s stated project reworks Marxian categories to investigate women’s oppression. D’Emilio’s separately checked historical inquiry concerns wages, family dependence and sexual identity; these are distinct uses.
strands.works: Marxism and the Oppression of Women (1983), description; Capitalism and Gay Identity (1983)

strands.title: Situated histories of class, slavery and liberation
strands.focus: Thompson, James and Rodney bring agency, enslavement, revolution and historical specificity to materialist inquiry. European conclusions cannot simply substitute for investigation of other histories.
strands.works: Making preface (1963); Black Jacobins lectures (1971); Marxism and African Liberation (1975)

strands.title: Intellectual functions, consent and organization
strands.focus: Gramsci distinguishes social intellectual functions from professional labels; organic is not a synonym for radical or morally preferable.

strands.title: Subaltern organization and historical traces
strands.focus: Gramsci proposes variable research dimensions, interrupted activity and difficult archival work; later colonial adaptations require separate evidence.

language.label: Linguistic turn / poststructuralism
language.description: Examines how language, narrative, discourse, and power shape historical knowledge and subject formation. Narrative theory, structuralist inheritances, and poststructuralist critiques overlap but are not interchangeable. This node groups debates rather than identifying one school.
language.representative_figures_and_works: Michel Foucault; Jacques Derrida; Hayden White, Metahistory (1973). Richard Rorty, ed.: The Linguistic Turn (1967).

representative_people.context: Discourse, genealogy and subject formation are related, changing inquiries; institutional and practical relations enter the account. Historians adapt and criticize them in different ways.
representative_people.works: The Archaeology of Knowledge (1969); “Nietzsche, Genealogy, History” (1971); “The Subject and Power” (1982)

representative_people.context: Questions conceptual hierarchies and conditions of signification through close reading and institutional questions; no mechanical rule permits arbitrary interpretation.
representative_people.works: Of Grammatology (1967); “Letter to a Japanese Friend” (1983); Archive Fever (1994/1996)

representative_people.context: Historical narrative theory; not every position under the linguistic turn.
representative_people.works: Metahistory (1973)

representative_people.context: Reworks signification and unconscious interpretation; the linguistic turn is not a uniform Lacanian program.
representative_people.works: “Le stade du miroir” (1949); “L’instance de la lettre” (1957); Écrits collection (1966)

representative_people.context: Theorizes material ideology and the constitution of subjects; reception is specifically documented through Hall and cultural-studies debates.
representative_people.works: “Ideology and Ideological State Apparatuses” (1970); Hall, “Cultural Studies: Two Paradigms” (1980)

representative_people.context: An interlocutor in historians’ reception of Foucault, organizing debate across theoretical and empirical approaches. The edited volume is not one uniform Foucauldian program.
representative_people.works: Foucault and the Writing of History, edited collection (1994); Console and Classify (1987)

representative_people.context: Derrida examines the relation of writing to the historicity of ideal objects through Husserl’s geometry. This is a particular critical engagement, not Husserl’s membership in a later historical turn.
representative_people.works: Husserl’s Origin of Geometry as discussed in Derrida, Of Grammatology (1967), chapter 2 opening

representative_people.context: Derrida explicitly identifies Destruktion and Abbau as resources that he adapts; the acknowledgment does not imply endorsement of Heidegger’s whole philosophy or politics.
representative_people.works: Derrida, “Letter to a Japanese Friend” (1983); Of Grammatology (1967), selected chapter 2

representative_people.context: Derrida explicitly draws on signs and interpretants while questioning a final meaning outside signification. This contextual use does not equate pragmatism with deconstruction.
representative_people.works: Peirce passages discussed in Derrida, Of Grammatology (1967), corrected English edition pp. 48–50

representative_people.context: An explicit resource in Foucault’s genealogy and Barthes’s discussion of facts and meaning; their appropriations are distinct from Nietzsche’s full argument.
representative_people.works: Genealogy (1887), selected passages; Foucault’s genealogy essay (1971); Barthes’s history essay (1967)

representative_people.context: Moves among myth analysis, historical discourse and a challenge to authorial closure. His trajectory is not a single timeless structuralist method.
representative_people.works: Mythologies (1957); “The Discourse of History” and “The Death of the Author” (1967); “The Reality Effect” (1968)

representative_people.context: Explicitly cited for dialogue among texts and paragrammatism in Barthes’s historical-discourse analysis. The original article is not newly read and the acknowledgment does not establish identical positions.
representative_people.works: “Bakhtine, le mot, le dialogue et le roman” (1967), cited in Barthes’s “The Discourse of History,” note 3

representative_people.context: Barthes invokes his research on ambiguous words in Greek tragedy to distinguish characters’ understanding from the spectator’s. This is a named scholarly resource, not a formal linguistic-turn affiliation.
representative_people.works: Research on Greek tragedy as invoked in “The Death of the Author” (1967), final paragraph

representative_people.context: A historian and translator who makes rhetorical analysis usable for historiography while retaining questions about sources and reference.
representative_people.works: Barthes translation (1981); “Analysing the discourse of history” (1983/1990)

representative_people.context: Reads texts as situated social acts with distinct discursive forms; manuscript and patronage evidence changed her initial hypothesis.
representative_people.works: Romancing the Past (1993), introduction, acknowledgments and notes

representative_people.context: Historicizes gender categories and the production of experience while retaining institutional relations and historical inquiry.
representative_people.works: “Gender” (1986); “The Evidence of Experience” (1991)

representative_people.context: Questions the political idioms through which class receives meaning; this is a particular historical intervention.
representative_people.works: Languages of Class (1983), selected introduction opening

representative_people.context: Reconsiders textual interpretation and the meaning of context through literary criticism and philosophy.
representative_people.works: Rethinking Intellectual History (1983)

representative_people.context: Investigates laboring people’s understandings of social order across politics, work, language and art.
representative_people.works: Visions of the People (1991)

representative_people.context: An interlocutor whose article explicitly frames meaning and experience as a historiographical problem; detailed argument remains to be checked.
representative_people.works: “Intellectual History after the Linguistic Turn” (1987)

representative_people.context: Spiegel explicitly credits her draft argument and sustained manuscript reading in developing a social/textual historical method.
representative_people.works: “The Body Politic” (1989), cited in Romancing the Past (1993), introduction note 7

representative_people.context: Socially situated discourse is an explicitly cited resource for Spiegel, not a formal affiliation with a later historians’ school.
representative_people.works: The Dialogic Imagination (English 1981), p. 259 cited by Spiegel (1993)

representative_people.context: White explicitly adapts a literary taxonomy while allowing alternatives.
representative_people.works: Anatomy of Criticism (1957)

representative_people.context: Named rhetorical resource in White’s introduction; distinct from Peter Burke and Edmund Burke III.
representative_people.works: A Grammar of Motives (edition cited by White1969)

representative_people.context: White discusses representation through a comparison with literary inquiry.
representative_people.works: Mimesis, cited by White in Metahistory (1973),2n1

representative_people.context: Develops a feminist response to Scott’s treatment of experience and agency.
representative_people.works: “Feminist History after the Linguistic Turn” (1994), 374–379

representative_people.context: Rorty’s anthology of analytic philosophers’ essays on philosophical method gave the phrase “the linguistic turn” wide currency. Historians’ linguistic turn drew mainly on other, often French, resources, so this records the name’s source, not a lineage.
representative_people.works: The Linguistic Turn (1967), ed.

strands.title: Discourse and genealogy
strands.focus: Archaeology examines rules connecting actual statements and the formation of objects; genealogy traces contingent descent and emergence. Social and institutional relations enter these inquiries.
strands.works: The Archaeology of Knowledge (1969), three chapters; “Nietzsche, Genealogy, History” (1971), pp. 139–152

strands.title: Deconstruction
strands.focus: Critical work through conceptual hierarchies and differential relations, with an explicitly adapted Heidegger resource. The 1983 letter rejects a mechanical method and includes institutions and translation.
strands.works: Of Grammatology (1967), selected chapter 2; “Letter to a Japanese Friend” (1983)

strands.title: Narrative theory
strands.focus: Emplotment and tropes concern the forms of historical explanation.

strands.title: Signification and divided subjectivity
strands.focus: Lacan’s changed sign diagram and reading of dream-work distinguish his appropriation from literal repetition of Saussure. Historians debate its capacity to explain changing gender relations.

strands.title: Ideology, practices and subjects
strands.focus: Althusser’s interpellation operates through material practices. His apparatuses include contradiction and resistance; Hall’s adoption and criticism remain a specific reception.

strands.title: Subject formation, action and resistance
strands.focus: Foucault distinguishes power relations from capacities and communication while studying their interconnections; freedom and resistance enter action upon actions. Goldstein provides a historically situated interlocutor.
strands.works: “The Subject and Power” (1982); Foucault and the Writing of History (1994)

strands.title: Writing, ideal objects and historicity
strands.focus: Derrida’s critical reading of Husserl asks how writing enters the historical transmission of ideal objects. It is distinct from a claim that historical evidence has no constraints.

strands.title: Interpretants and a critique of presence
strands.focus: Peirce is a named resource in Derrida’s account of signification; this particular use neither subsumes all pragmatism nor equates arbitrariness with individual caprice.
strands.works: Of Grammatology, corrected English edition (1997), pp. 44–50

strands.title: Madness, reason and discursive practice
strands.focus: Derrida questions the language of an archaeology of silence; Foucault disputes his reading of Descartes and the reduction of discursive practices to textual traces. Each criticism remains attributed.
strands.works: “Cogito and the History of Madness” (lecture 1963); “My Body, This Paper, This Fire” (English 1979)

strands.title: Genealogical questions and perspectival knowledge
strands.focus: Nietzsche’s distinction between origins and uses, and his account of multiple perspectives, enter different later arguments in Foucault and Barthes. Their readings are not interchangeable.
strands.works: Genealogy II.12–13 and III.12; Foucault (1971); Barthes (1967)

strands.title: Myth and the naturalization of history
strands.focus: Barthes’s two-level account asks how historically produced meanings appear natural. He links formal analysis with historical criticism, rather than treating semiology as sufficient by itself.

strands.title: Authorship, textual plurality and the reader
strands.focus: The 1967 essay questions the author as final explanatory authority and invokes Vernant’s tragic ambiguity. Its theoretical reader must be distinguished from research on actual readers.
strands.works: “The Death of the Author” (1967), Richard Howard translation

strands.title: Historical utterance, reference and narrative detail
strands.focus: Barthes distinguishes acts of uttering, content units and signification, drawing on Jakobson and Kristeva. Bann’s adoption and qualification keep historical practice within the debate.
strands.works: “The Discourse of History” (1967); “The Reality Effect” (1968); Bann (1983/1990)

strands.title: Social sites and textual action
strands.focus: Spiegel combines attention to form with documentary and patronage inquiry; texts act in social settings and are not transparent reflections.

strands.title: Gender categories and historical experience
strands.focus: Scott makes experience something to explain and connects meanings with institutions and subjectivity.

strands.title: Class and political idioms
strands.focus: Different historical inquiries question how social identities receive political meaning.
strands.works: Languages of Class (1983); Visions of the People (1991)

strands.title: Texts, contexts and debates over experience
strands.focus: LaCapra’s textual/contextual project and Toews’s explicitly titled meaning/experience intervention are distinct; detailed agreement is not presumed.
strands.works: Rethinking Intellectual History (1983); Intellectual History after the Linguistic Turn (1987)

strands.title: Literary taxonomies and historical events
strands.focus: White distinguishes narrative arrangement from invented events and treats plot classifications as revisable analytical choices.

language.scope_note: Structural linguistics, discourse, deconstruction, and narrative theory differ. A historical concern with language alone does not identify a poststructuralist.

liberal_order_framework.label: Liberal order framework
liberal_order_framework.date_label: State-formation roots: Curtis 1988, Greer and Radforth 1992 · McKay’s prospectus Dec. 2000 · debate volume 2009 · selected later readings
liberal_order_framework.description: A proposal to write Canadian history as the history of a liberal project of rule. Ian McKay's prospectus in the Canadian Historical Review (2000) offered a way past the impasse between socio-cultural and national-political history: map 'Canada' as the project through which liberal order (in Fecteau's paraphrase, an individualism of liberty, equality and property) became common sense in northern North America from the 1840s. Commentators identify Gramsci's hegemony and Fernande Roy's study of francophone business liberalism as its sources and link it to earlier state-formation research: Bruce Curtis on schooling and the census, and Allan Greer and Ian Radforth's Colonial Leviathan (1992). Constant and Ducharme's Liberalism and Hegemony (2009) tested it on rights, municipalities, conservation, families, women and racialized people, and First Nations. This entry reads the framework as closer to a history of capitalism than to moral regulation: its subject is how property, the individual and market relations became the terms of rule. In his 2009 reply McKay held that liberal order and capitalism cannot be conflated, yet after the 1840s could not easily be separated. Earlier social histories of seigneurial Quebec (Greer 1985) and Montreal's wage-earning families (Bradbury 1993) are read alongside it. Critics answered: Bryan Palmer argued that the framework sidesteps capitalism's changing structures. Jerry Bannister proposed a loyalist order before 1840. Ruth Sandwell found a-liberal families, and Nancy Christie faulted its neglect of religion and of women. Later histories of land, enclosure and taxation (Weaver, Greer, Heaman) carry its questions further.
liberal_order_framework.representative_figures_and_works: Roots: Curtis, Building the Educational State (1988), True Government by Choice Men? (1992), The Politics of Population (2001); Greer and Radforth, eds., Colonial Leviathan (1992). Prospectus: McKay, “The Liberal Order Framework” (CHR, 2000), drawing on Roy, Progrès, harmonie, liberté (1988). Debate: Sandwell (2003); Constant and Ducharme, eds., Liberalism and Hegemony (2009), with Bannister, Heaman, Curtis, Sandwell, Perry, Brownlie and McKay’s reply; the Underhill Review round table (Ajzenstat, Christie, Fecteau, Pâquet) and Palmer (2009). Liberty: Ducharme (2010), McNairn (2000). Transition to capitalism (read alongside): Greer, Peasant, Lord, and Merchant (1985); Bradbury, Working Families (1993). Property and capitalism: Weaver (2003), Greer (2012, 2018), Heaman (2017). Left history: McKay (2005, 2008).
liberal_order_framework.scope_note: A programme and its debate rather than a school: roster inclusion is not adoption. Curtis, Greer and Radforth wrote its roots before it was named; Christie, Palmer, Sandwell, Fecteau and Ajzenstat appear as critics; Bannister proposes a loyalist order for 1750–1840 (chapter title), its relation to McKay not characterized. Kept separate from moral regulation by the user (2026-10-12) as "a different project closer to history of capitalism"; that reading is editorial and is stated as such in the description. The overlap with histories of capitalism is noted in the description; it is not drawn as a link, because the fields have not connected (user, 2026-10-12). Greer (1985) and Bradbury (1993) are read alongside the framework, not as its roots or applications.

strands.title: State formation before the framework

Curtis (1988) and Greer and Radforth (1992) predate the prospectus; Curtis's later books (2001, 2012) continue that work, and their relation to the framework is not checked here.

strands.title: The prospectus: Canada as a project of liberal rule
strands.focus: McKay proposes mapping Canada as liberal hegemony to get past the social versus national-political impasse. Pâquet names Gramsci and Fernande Roy as its explicit sources.
strands.works: McKay, “The Liberal Order Framework” (2000); Roy, Progrès, harmonie, liberté (1988)

strands.title: Property, market society and capitalism
strands.focus: The editorial reason for separating this entry from moral regulation: the framework's individual is a property-holder, and its later work runs to land, enclosure and taxation. McKay distinguishes liberal order from capitalism; Palmer replies that the distinction lets historians avoid capitalism.
strands.works: McKay, “Canada as a Long Liberal Revolution” (2009); Weaver, The Great Land Rush (2003); Greer, “Commons and Enclosure” (2012) and Property and Dispossession (2018); Heaman, Tax, Order, and Good Government (2017)

strands.title: Liberty, public opinion and francophone liberalisms
strands.focus: Intellectual histories of liberty and deliberation that test whether "liberalism" was one thing: republican against modern liberty in the two Canadas, public opinion in Upper Canada, francophone business liberalism.
strands.works: Ducharme, Le concept de liberté au Canada (2010); McNairn, The Capacity to Judge (2000) and “In Hope and Fear” (2009); Roy (1988)

strands.title: Debating the Canadian liberal revolution
strands.focus: The 2009 volume tests the framework across rights, municipalities, conservation, the family, women and racialized people, First Nations and British Columbia; McKay replies with a long liberal revolution of the 1840s–1940s.
strands.works: Constant and Ducharme, eds., Liberalism and Hegemony (2009)

strands.title: Critiques
strands.focus: a-liberal families (Sandwell); religion, gender and governmentality (Christie); capitalism avoided (Palmer); an unstable definition (Fecteau); thin primary evidence (Ajzenstat).
strands.works: Sandwell (2003, 2009); Bannister (2009); the Underhill Review round table (2009): Ajzenstat, Christie, Fecteau, Pâquet; Palmer (2009)

strands.title: The left as counter-project
strands.focus: McKay's history of Canadian socialist and left "formations" measures the left by how far it pushed liberal order "to its definitional limits" (as Palmer quotes him).
strands.works: McKay, Rebels, Reds, Radicals (2005); Reasoning Otherwise (2008)

strands.title: Rural society, wage labour and the transition to capitalism
strands.focus: Social histories on either side of the transition, read alongside the framework in Canadian PhDs (Bradbury: 13 of 44 citing PhDs also cite McKay 2000, lift 4.0; Greer: 5 of 16, lift 4.2). Greer finds habitant society in the Lower Richelieu, 1740–1840, organized around a feudal order with household self-sufficiency; Bradbury follows Montreal working-class families as wage labour and industrial capitalism remade family survival. Both predate the prospectus and are not checked as responses to it.
strands.works: Greer, Peasant, Lord, and Merchant (1985); Bradbury, Working Families (1993)

cdn_working_class.label: Canadian working-class history
cdn_working_class.date_label: Earlier institutional histories (Logan 1948) · Labour/Le Travailleur founded 1976 · Palmer 1979, Kealey 1980 · debate over culture 1981 · gender and family 1989–93 · selected later works
cdn_working_class.description: Canadian working-class history took shape in the 1970s as a new labour history of class, culture and community, set against an older institutional history of unions, labour politics and industrial relations (Logan 1948; Abella 1973; Bercuson 1974). The Canadian Committee on Labour History founded Labour/Le Travailleur in 1976. Palmer’s skilled workers in Hamilton (1979), Kealey’s Toronto workers (1980) and their history of the Knights of Labor (1982) were among its early monographs. In 1981 Kenneth McNaught framed the contrast as ‘E. P. Thompson vs Harold Logan’ and, by a later account, objected that social historians took a revolutionary goal as history’s purpose; Bercuson questioned working-class culture as an explanatory framework, and Kealey defended class analysis and culture. Social historians of poverty and the state widened the field: Copp’s Montreal working class (1974), Finkel on business and reform (1979), Struthers on unemployment (1983). Feminist historians remade it from within: Sangster on women on the left (1989), Parr’s gender of breadwinners (1990) and Bradbury’s working families (1993). Rouillard wrote the history of Quebec unionism in French (1989), and Heron’s Workers’ Revolt in Canada (1998) took the 1917–25 upheaval as a national subject. Palmer’s Descent into Discourse (1990) attacked the linguistic turn in social history. In 2000 Morton argued that the journal’s founding team had concealed a decade of stasis. Later work turned to deindustrialization (High 2003), the history of the left (McKay 2008) and Indigenous labour and the settler order.
cdn_working_class.representative_figures_and_works: Logan, Trade Unions in Canada (1948); Abella, Nationalism, Communism, and Canadian Labour (1973); Bercuson, Confrontation at Winnipeg (1974); Copp, The Anatomy of Poverty (1974); Labour/Le Travailleur (1976); Palmer, A Culture in Conflict (1979); Finkel, Business and Social Reform in the Thirties (1979); Kealey, Toronto Workers Respond to Industrial Capitalism (1980); McNaught, Bercuson and Kealey (1981); Kealey and Palmer, Dreaming of What Might Be (1982); Struthers, No Fault of Their Own (1983); Palmer, Working-Class Experience (1983; 1992); Heron, Working in Steel (1988); Rouillard, Histoire du syndicalisme au Québec (1989); Sangster, Dreams of Equality (1989); Palmer, Descent into Discourse (1990); Parr, The Gender of Breadwinners (1990); Lutz, “After the Fur Trade” (1992); Bradbury, Working Families (1993); Kealey, Workers and Canadian History (1995); Heron, The Workers’ Revolt in Canada (1998); Morton and Sangster in Labour/Le Travail 46 (2000). Later: High, Industrial Sunset (2003); McKay, Reasoning Otherwise (2008); Burrill (2019); Finkel on Palmer (2021).
cdn_working_class.scope_note: A national research field within labour history. The ‘old’ institutional history and the ‘new’ labour history are positions in a debate, not successive stages; Bercuson and McNaught are critics (their 1981 essays are now checked through Bercuson’s abstract and Finkel’s account of McNaught), and Morton’s 2000 critique comes from outside the new labour history. Marxist and Thompsonian resources are documented by McNaught’s title and Kealey’s defence of class analysis; no single theory is attributed to the field. Gender historians (Sangster, Parr, Bradbury) are treated mainly in Canadian women’s and gender history; they appear here for their working-class histories. Quebec labour history in French (Rouillard) is part of the field and of Quebec historiography. Poverty and welfare-state histories overlap with political history. Immigrant workers (Avery) are in the immigration entry; Indigenous labour is a strand, not a claim of adoption. Palmer’s Descent into Discourse (1990) is placed here as a critique of the linguistic turn, not as a critique of women’s history. McKay’s left history is a post-2000 contributor row; his main entry is Liberal order framework.

strands.title: Unions, labour politics and industrial relations
strands.focus: Logan’s history of unions (1948), Abella on the CIO, communism and nationalism (1973), and Bercuson on the Winnipeg General Strike (1974): the institutional history against which the new labour history defined itself.

strands.title: The new labour history: class, culture and community
strands.focus: Palmer’s skilled workers in Hamilton (1979), Kealey’s Toronto workers (1980), their Knights of Labor (1982) and Palmer’s synthesis (1983; 1992). Kealey also engages the US new labour history of Gutman and Montgomery (1990, title-level).

strands.title: Labour/Le Travail and the CCLH
strands.focus: The Canadian Committee on Labour History founded Labour/Le Travailleur in 1976: the journal’s archive and Crossref date volume 1 to 1976, with Palmer, Kealey and Rouillard (in French) among its contributors. Freeman names Kealey, Palmer and Sangster among the founding generation. The journal is also the site of the 1981 and 2000 exchanges.

strands.title: The 1981 debate over culture and class
strands.focus: McNaught frames the decade as ‘E. P. Thompson vs Harold Logan’ (CHR 1981) and, by Finkel’s account, objects that social historians took a revolutionary goal as the purpose of historical writing. In Labour/Le Travailleur 7, Bercuson questions working-class culture as an explanatory framework and the priority of history “from the bottom up”; Kealey strongly defends class analysis and culture. Kealey’s collected essays (1995) reprint his reply. McNaught’s essay is read only through Finkel.

strands.title: Poverty, unemployment and the welfare state
strands.focus: Copp’s Montreal working class (1974), Finkel on business and social reform (1979) and Struthers on unemployment and the welfare state (1983).

strands.title: Gender, family and class
strands.focus: Women on the left (Sangster 1989), the gender of breadwinners (Parr 1990) and working families (Bradbury 1993). Sangster (2000) describes feminist challenges to the initially ‘masculinist’ shape of working-class history and calls to integrate race and ethnicity.

strands.title: Quebec labour history
strands.focus: Rouillard’s history of Quebec unionism (1989) in French; Copp and Bradbury on Montreal’s working class. Shared with Quebec historiography.

strands.title: Steel, revolt and national scope
strands.focus: Heron’s steelworkers (1988) and The Workers’ Revolt in Canada, 1917–1925 (1998), a national frame for the post-war upheaval (title-level).

strands.title: Discourse, stasis and critique, 1990–2000
strands.focus: Palmer’s Descent into Discourse (1990) attacks the reification of language in social history, a critique of the linguistic turn (Finkel). Morton (2000) argues the L/LT team’s domination concealed stasis and decline; Sangster (2000) records the feminist critique and the unsettling effect of post-structuralism and the left’s decline.

strands.title: Indigenous labour and the settler order
strands.focus: Lutz (1992) treats Aboriginal people in British Columbia as a labouring class. Burrill (2019, after 2000) proposes a settler-order framework that puts settler workers’ ongoing theft of Indigenous land into Canadian working-class history.

strands.title: Deindustrialization
strands.focus: High’s cross-border history of plant closures, 1969–84 (2003), after the main period.

strands.title: Histories of the Canadian left (after 2000)
strands.focus: McKay’s Reasoning Otherwise (2008), first of a planned three-volume history of the left from 1890 to the Winnipeg General Strike; read by many PhDs who engage working-class history.
